a.label: Carve-Out Provision (DCSA relief from NISP oversight)

edges.label: the provision that removes a contractor facility from the government's own industrial security oversight
edges.note: Defined in DoD Directive 5205.07 and DoD Manual 5205.07 Volume 1 as a provision approved by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense relieving the defence security agency of its National Industrial Security Program oversight responsibilities at a contractor facility. It is the structural seam at which a programme held at a company stops being visible to any government security official outside the programme.

a.label: Congressional oversight of special access programs

edges.label: the statutory oversight scheme, and the exception written into it
edges.note: Under 10 U.S.C. 119 the Secretary must report annually by 1 March to the four defense committees on every special access program, with a brief description, major milestones and costs - and under 119(e) may waive any of that on a case-by-case basis. The scheme and its exception are the same statute, which is why oversight belongs on the structural map rather than outside it.

a.label: DoD Special Access Program Central Office (DoD SAPCO)

edges.label: the office that holds the Department's SAP portfolio and is its single point of contact to Congress
edges.note: Established by DoD Directive 5205.07 (reissued 12 September 2024) 'under the authority, direction, and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense', with a Director who must be a general or flag officer or SES equivalent, and designated the primary DoD liaison with the Executive Branch and Congress on all DoD SAP issues. Any structural map of where a legacy programme could sit starts at this node.

edges.note: OUSD(I), since 2020 OUSD(I&S), is where the sensitive-activities policy authority sits and where the whole Elizondo/AATIP dispute takes place. It is also the office under which the Military Intelligence Program is managed, which makes it the point where this domain's organisational and funding threads meet.

edges.label: the four-member channel that 10 U.S.C. 119(e) substitutes for committee reporting
edges.note: Sec. 119(e)(2) directs that where the Secretary exercises the waiver, the information and the justification go jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees - the Armed Services and Appropriations committees of both chambers. Attaching this node to the structural domain is what stops the two channels being conflated. [Corrected 14 Aug 2026: 10 U.S.C. 119(g) defines 'defense committees' as SIX bodies including both Appropriations Defense subcommittees, so notification runs to twelve seats, not eight. Section 119 uses its own definition, not 10 U.S.C. 101(a)(16).]

a.label: Waived unacknowledged special access program (waived USAP)

edges.label: the access category whose costs reach four members rather than four committees
edges.note: Unacknowledged existence (DoDI 5205.11 glossary), waived congressional reporting under 10 U.S.C. 119(e), and carve-out relief from industrial security oversight combine to produce an activity that is funded but not reconcilable from any public document. Every element is sourced to a statute or a DoD issuance rather than to an allegation; the inference that a legacy programme uses this stack is not.
